subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Open your eyes at dawn and the world appears. The pink glow over the savanna after the Gu rains, the silver flash of sunlight on the Indian Ocean, the deep green of a mango leaf, the golden lamp of the crescent moon that marks the start of a new lunar month, the letters on this very page, all of it reaches you because of one thing: light. Light is a form of energy that your eyes can detect. Without it, there is no seeing. In this unit you will learn how light travels, how it bounces off mirrors and the sea, how it bends as it passes into a glass of water, how lenses and your own eye focus it, and how white sunlight is secretly a mixture of every colour of the rainbow.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Describe reflection at a plane surface and use the law of reflection.
Describe refraction of light at the boundary between air and glass or air and water in terms of change of speed.
Know that white light is made of many colours and this can be shown through the dispersion of white light, using a prism.
Describe how colours of light can be added, subtracted, absorbed and reflected.
Take appropriately accurate and precise measurements, explaining why accuracy and precision are important.

outcomes: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
Explain that light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines and describe evidence for this, such as shadows and beams.
Describe the difference between luminous and non-luminous objects and explain how we see non-luminous objects by reflected light.
State and use the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Measure angles of incidence and reflection from the normal and solve simple numerical problems.
Explain refraction as the bending of light when it changes speed passing from one material into another.
Describe how convex and concave lenses bend light, and explain how a converging lens forms an image.
Label the main parts of the human eye and explain how the eye focuses light onto the retina.
Explain dispersion and how a prism or rain droplets split white light into a spectrum.
Describe the difference between mixing coloured light and mixing paints, and explain why objects appear the colours they do.

concepts.title: How Light Travels
concepts.explanation:
Light is a form of energy. Like sound and heat, it can travel from one place to another. But unlike sound, light does not need a material to travel through. Sound cannot cross empty space, yet sunlight crosses millions of kilometres of empty space to reach us. That is why the sun can warm your face across all that emptiness.

The most important fact about light is this: light travels in straight lines. We call these straight paths rays. Think of the thin, sharp beams of sunlight that slice through a gap in the roof of a house in Hargeisa on a dusty morning, or the headlights of a lorry cutting straight through the dark on the road to Garissa. The beam never curves around a corner by itself. This single idea explains a great deal.

Here is the strongest everyday evidence that light travels in straight lines: shadows. When Amina stands in the bright afternoon sun, her body blocks the light. Because light cannot bend around her, the ground behind her is left dark in the exact shape of her body. That dark patch is her shadow. If light could curve around her, there would be no sharp shadow at all. An object that blocks light completely, like Amina, a wall, or a goat, is called opaque. An object that lets light pass straight through, like clean window glass or clear water, is called transparent. Some objects, like thin cloth or frosted glass, let some light through but scatter it, so you cannot see clearly through them; we call these translucent.

Light also travels incredibly fast, about 300,000 kilometres every second. That is so fast it could circle the whole earth more than seven times in a single second. This is why, when you switch on a torch, the light seems to reach the far wall instantly. Sound is far slower, which is why in a thunderstorm over the Rift Valley you see the flash of lightning first and hear the thunder several seconds later, even though both happen at the same moment.

Some objects make their own light. We call them luminous. The sun is the greatest luminous object in our sky. A fire, a torch bulb, a candle, and a firefly glowing at dusk are all luminous. Most objects, however, make no light of their own. We call these non-luminous. A goat, a tree, this page, and the moon itself are all non-luminous. So how do you see them?

You see a non-luminous object because light from a luminous source lands on it, bounces off it, and travels into your eyes. When you look at a mango on a market stall in Mogadishu, sunlight strikes the mango, reflects off its skin, and enters your eye. The mango is not glowing; it is simply reflecting the sun's light to you. The moon is the perfect example: it looks bright, but it makes no light at all. It is a giant non-luminous rock reflecting sunlight back to earth. The beautiful crescent that announces the start of Ramadan is sunlight bouncing off the moon.

Did You Know? The light you see from the sun left it about eight minutes ago. If the sun suddenly went dark, you would keep seeing sunlight for eight more minutes before the sky went black. Light is fast, but space is huge.
concepts.example: It is worth pausing on one more idea before we move on. Because light travels in straight lines, we can predict exactly where a shadow will fall and how big it will be. When Farah stands close to a wall in the low morning sun, her shadow is short and sharp. As the sun climbs and then sinks again towards evening, the same shadow stretches long across the ground. The shadow is always a faithful map of where the straight rays are blocked. People have used this for thousands of years: a simple upright stick, its shadow tracking the sun across the day, was one of the earliest clocks. The regular movement of light and shadow, like the phases of the moon that mark the months, is part of the ordered pattern of creation that careful observers have always noticed.

concepts.title: Reflection and the Law of Reflection
concepts.explanation:
When light hits a surface and bounces off, we call it reflection. Every surface reflects at least some light, which is why you can see it at all. A very smooth, shiny surface like a mirror or the calm surface of the Indian Ocean at dawn reflects light in an orderly way, so it can form a clear image. A rough surface like a wall or a dusty road reflects light in all directions and scatters it, so it shows no image. Both are reflection; the difference is only how smooth the surface is.

To describe reflection precisely, scientists do not measure angles from the mirror itself. Instead they draw an imaginary line straight out of the surface, at exactly 90 degrees to it, at the point where the ray hits. This line is called the normal. It is your reference line. You measure every angle from the normal, never from the mirror.

The ray arriving at the mirror is the incident ray.

The ray bouncing away is the reflected ray.

The angle of incidence (often written as the letter i) is between the incident ray and the normal.

The angle of reflection (written as r) is between the reflected ray and the normal.

Now here is one of the most reliable rules in all of science, the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. In short, i = r. If light strikes a mirror at 30 degrees from the normal, it leaves at exactly 30 degrees from the normal on the other side. It never changes. This law is always true for every flat mirror, every time, everywhere.

Worked Example: using the law of reflection

Let us work through a problem step by step, the way you should in your notebook. Hassan shines a torch at a flat mirror. The incident ray hits the mirror so that it makes an angle of 50 degrees with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?

Find the angle of incidence first. The angle is given from the mirror surface, but we must measure from the normal. The normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror. So the angle of incidence = 90 — 50 = 40 degrees.

Apply the law of reflection. The law says angle of incidence = angle of reflection, so i = r.

State the answer. Since i = 40 degrees, the angle of reflection r = 40 degrees (measured from the normal).

Check it makes sense. The reflected ray also makes 90 — 40 = 50 degrees with the mirror surface, mirroring the incident ray perfectly. That is exactly what we expect from a flat mirror.

Let us try a second one. A ray strikes a mirror with an angle of incidence of 25 degrees. What is the angle of reflection, and what is the total angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray? By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection is also 25 degrees. The two rays sit on opposite sides of the normal, so the total angle between them is 25 + 25 = 50 degrees. Notice the pattern: the angle between the two rays is always double the angle of incidence.

When Khadija looks into a flat mirror, she sees an image of herself that is the same size as she is, standing the same distance behind the mirror as she is in front of it, and the right way up. But the image is laterally inverted, which means left and right are swapped. Raise your right hand in front of a mirror and your image raises what looks like its left hand. This is why the word on the front of an ambulance is often printed backwards, so that a driver ahead sees it the right way round in their rear-view mirror.
concepts.example: There are two kinds of reflection worth naming. When light reflects off a smooth surface like a still pool or a polished mirror, all the rays bounce off in the same orderly direction, and we call this regular reflection; it gives a clear image. When light reflects off a rough surface like a wall, a dusty road, or the bark of an acacia tree, the tiny bumps face in every direction, so the rays scatter every which way. This is called diffuse reflection, and it gives no image. Diffuse reflection is actually very useful: it is exactly why you can see this page from any angle, because the paper scatters light towards your eyes wherever you sit. Without diffuse reflection the whole world would be a confusing hall of mirrors.

concepts.title: Refraction: When Light Bends
concepts.explanation:
Light travels fastest in empty space and in air. When it passes into a denser transparent material like water or glass, it slows down. And here is the surprising result: when light slows down as it enters a new material at an angle, it changes direction. It bends. This bending of light as it changes speed passing from one material into another is called refraction.

You have seen refraction countless times. Put a straw or a spoon into a glass of water and look from the side. The straw appears bent or broken at the surface of the water. The straw is perfectly straight, of course. What has bent is the light coming from the underwater part of the straw. As that light leaves the water and enters the air, it refracts, and your eyes are fooled into thinking the straw is snapped. The same effect makes a swimming pool or a river look shallower than it really is, and makes a fish in the water appear to be in a slightly different place than it actually is, which is a real challenge for anyone spearing fish along the coast near Kismaayo.

There is a simple rule to remember the direction of bending, using the normal as before:

When light passes from a less dense material into a more dense material (air into water or glass), it slows down and bends towards the normal.

When light passes from a more dense material into a less dense material (water or glass into air), it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

If the ray hits the surface straight on, exactly along the normal, it does not bend at all; it only slows down. Bending happens only when light strikes the surface at an angle.

Have you ever seen what looks like a shining pool of water on the road ahead on a hot afternoon, only for it to vanish as you get closer? That is a mirage, and it is caused by refraction. On a scorching day the air just above the tarmac becomes very hot and thin, while the air higher up is cooler and denser. Light from the sky travelling down towards the road bends gradually as it passes through these layers of air of different density, until it curves upward into your eyes. Your brain assumes the light travelled in a straight line, so it places an image of the bright sky on the ground, and you see what looks like a puddle of water. It is not water at all; it is refracted skylight.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Because light bends as it enters our atmosphere, the sun is actually already below the horizon at the moment you see it set. Refraction lifts its image up, giving you a couple of extra minutes of sunset each evening over the ocean.

concepts.title: How Lenses Work
concepts.explanation:
A lens is a carefully shaped piece of clear glass or plastic that uses refraction to bend light in a useful way. Because a lens is curved, light rays passing through different parts of it bend by different amounts, and this lets a lens gather light together or spread it apart. There are two main kinds.

A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges. It bends parallel rays of light inward so that they meet at a single point. Because it brings light together, it is also called a converging lens. The point where the rays meet is called the focus or focal point. A magnifying glass is a convex lens; hold one over a page and it makes the letters look larger. (You may also have noticed a magnifying glass can focus sunlight into a tiny hot spot bright enough to burn paper, which is a warning to handle the sun's light with great respect.)

A concave lens is thinner in the middle than at the edges. It bends parallel rays outward so they spread apart, as if they came from a point behind the lens. Because it spreads light out, it is called a diverging lens. Concave lenses are used to help people who are short-sighted see distant objects clearly.
concepts.example: When light from an object passes through a convex lens, the rays are bent and cross over to form an image on the other side. If Yusuf holds a convex lens up and lets it focus the scene from the window onto a white wall, he will see a small, upside-down picture of the outside world projected on the wall. This is a real image, because the light rays actually meet to form it and it can be caught on a screen. A camera works in exactly this way, and, as you will see next, so does your own eye. When the object is very close to the lens, as when you use it as a magnifying glass, the lens instead makes a larger, right-way-up image that you cannot catch on a screen.

concepts.title: The Human Eye
concepts.explanation:
Your eye is a living, natural camera, a beautifully made instrument for detecting light. Let us follow a ray of light from a mango on the stall into your eye and see how you form a picture of it.

The clear, curved front window of the eye.

Does most of the bending of incoming light.

The black hole in the centre that lets light in.

Looks black because it is a dark opening.

The coloured ring of muscle around the pupil.

Changes the pupil size to control how much light enters.

Fine-focuses light onto the retina; changes shape.

The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.

Where the image forms; full of light-detecting cells.

Turns light signals into a message the brain reads.
concepts.example: Here is the journey of the light. First, light from the mango passes through the clear cornea, which begins to bend it. It then passes through the pupil, the opening whose size is controlled by the coloured iris. In the bright equatorial midday sun the iris makes the pupil small to protect the eye; in a dim room at night it opens the pupil wide to let in more light. Next the light passes through the lens, a convex lens that can change shape to fine-focus the image. The lens and cornea together focus the light to form a small, upside-down real image on the retina at the back of the eye. The retina is packed with cells that detect the light and send signals along the optic nerve to the brain. Your clever brain flips the image the right way up, and you 'see' the mango. All of this happens in an instant, every moment your eyes are open.

concepts.title: Dispersion: The Hidden Colours of White Light
concepts.explanation:
White sunlight does not look coloured, yet it holds a secret. It is actually a mixture of every colour blended together. We can prove this by splitting it apart. When white light passes through a triangular block of glass called a prism, it spreads out into a band of colours. This splitting of white light into its separate colours is called dispersion, and the band of colours is called the spectrum.

The colours always come out in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Dispersion happens because each colour refracts, or bends, by a slightly different amount as it passes through the glass. Red light bends the least and violet light bends the most, so the colours fan out and separate.
concepts.example: The colours always come out in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Dispersion happens because each colour refracts, or bends, by a slightly different amount as it passes through the glass. Red light bends the least and violet light bends the most, so the colours fan out and separate.

methods.title: Does Light Travel in Straight Lines?
methods.example: To find evidence that light travels in straight lines.
steps: Make a small hole in the centre of each card at exactly the same height, using the pencil.
Stand the three cards up in a row, evenly spaced, with all three holes lined up straight.
In a darkened room, shine the torch through the first hole and look from the far side. Record whether the light reaches your eye.
Now slide the middle card sideways so its hole is no longer lined up with the others.
Shine the torch again and record whether the light still reaches your eye.

methods.title: The Law of Reflection with a Mirror
methods.example: To test whether the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
steps: Lay the paper flat and stand the mirror upright on it. Draw a line along the base of the mirror.
Draw the normal: a dotted line at 90 degrees to the mirror line, at the point the beam will hit.
In a dark room, shine the thin beam at that point at an angle. Mark two dots along the incoming beam and two along the reflected beam with your pencil.
Remove the mirror and torch. Use the ruler to join the dots into rays that meet at the point on the mirror line.
Measure the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection from the normal. Record both.

methods.title: The Bent Straw (Refraction in Water)
methods.example: To observe refraction and see how water bends light.
steps: Fill the glass about three-quarters full with clean water.
Stand the straw in the glass and look at it from the side, roughly at the level of the water.
Draw exactly what you see. Note where the straw appears to bend.
Now place a coin at the bottom of a bowl. Move back until the rim just hides the coin from view.
Keeping still, ask someone to slowly pour water into the bowl. Watch the coin.

methods.title: Splitting Light into a Rainbow
methods.example: To split white light into a spectrum and prove white light is a mixture of colours.
steps: Place the tray of water where sunlight from a window reaches it.
Slide the mirror into the water, leaning it against one side at an angle.
Adjust the mirror so sunlight strikes the underwater part and reflects up onto the white paper or wall.
The wedge of water in front of the mirror acts as a prism. Look for a band of colours on the paper.
Record the colours you see and their order.

methods.title: Why Objects Have Colour
methods.example: To investigate how the colour of the light changes the colour we see.
steps: Cover the torch with a red wrapper to make a red beam.
In a dark room, shine the red light on each coloured cloth in turn and record its apparent colour.
Repeat with a blue wrapper, then a green wrapper.
Note especially what happens to a cloth whose colour is NOT in the light you are shining.

workedExamples.title: using the law of reflection
workedExamples.prompt: Let us work through a problem step by step, the way you should in your notebook. Hassan shines a torch at a flat mirror. The incident ray hits the mirror so that it makes an angle of 50 degrees with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?
workedExamples.solution:
Find the angle of incidence first. The angle is given from the mirror surface, but we must measure from the normal. The normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror. So the angle of incidence = 90 — 50 = 40 degrees.

Check it makes sense. The reflected ray also makes 90 — 40 = 50 degrees with the mirror surface, mirroring the incident ray perfectly. That is exactly what we expect from a flat mirror.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a luminous object? (a) the moon (b) a mirror (c) the sun (d) a mango
workedExamples.solution: (c) the sun. A luminous object makes its own light; the moon, a mirror and a mango only reflect light.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Light travels in: (a) curves (b) straight lines (c) circles (d) zig-zags on its own
workedExamples.solution: (b) straight lines. This is shown by sharp shadows and narrow beams.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: The imaginary line at 90 degrees to a mirror is called the: (a) ray (b) normal (c) incident line (d) spectrum
workedExamples.solution: (b) normal. The normal is drawn at 90 degrees to the surface and is the reference for all angles.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of: (a) refraction (b) reflection (c) the mirror (d) dispersion
workedExamples.solution: (b) reflection. The law states angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: A ray hits a mirror at 30 degrees to the normal. The angle of reflection is: (a) 60 degrees (b) 30 degrees (c) 90 degrees (d) 15 degrees
workedExamples.solution: (b) 30 degrees. By the law of reflection the reflected angle equals the incident angle.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: The bending of light as it passes from air into water is called: (a) reflection (b) refraction (c) dispersion (d) scattering
workedExamples.solution: (b) refraction. Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed between materials.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: A convex lens is: (a) thinner in the middle (b) thicker in the middle (c) flat (d) always black
workedExamples.solution: (b) thicker in the middle. A convex (converging) lens is thicker at its centre.

activities.title: Does Light Travel in Straight Lines?
activities.materials: Three pieces of card or stiff paper (a cereal box works well); A torch or a phone torch; A pencil, a ruler, and some sticky tack or small lumps of dough to stand the cards up
steps: Make a small hole in the centre of each card at exactly the same height, using the pencil.
Stand the three cards up in a row, evenly spaced, with all three holes lined up straight.
In a darkened room, shine the torch through the first hole and look from the far side. Record whether the light reaches your eye.
Now slide the middle card sideways so its hole is no longer lined up with the others.
Shine the torch again and record whether the light still reaches your eye.
Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: The Law of Reflection with a Mirror
activities.materials: A small flat mirror stood upright against a book; A torch (cover the front with paper that has a thin slit cut in it to make a narrow beam); A sheet of paper, a ruler, a pencil, and a protractor if you have one
steps: Lay the paper flat and stand the mirror upright on it. Draw a line along the base of the mirror.
Draw the normal: a dotted line at 90 degrees to the mirror line, at the point the beam will hit.
In a dark room, shine the thin beam at that point at an angle. Mark two dots along the incoming beam and two along the reflected beam with your pencil.
Remove the mirror and torch. Use the ruler to join the dots into rays that meet at the point on the mirror line.
Measure the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection from the normal. Record both.

activities.title: The Bent Straw (Refraction in Water)
activities.materials: A clear glass or jar; Clean water; A straight straw, a pencil, or a spoon; A coin and a bowl (for the second part)
steps: Fill the glass about three-quarters full with clean water.
Stand the straw in the glass and look at it from the side, roughly at the level of the water.
Draw exactly what you see. Note where the straw appears to bend.
Now place a coin at the bottom of a bowl. Move back until the rim just hides the coin from view.
Keeping still, ask someone to slowly pour water into the bowl. Watch the coin.

activities.title: Splitting Light into a Rainbow
activities.materials: A shallow tray or bowl of water; A small flat mirror; A sheet of white paper or a white wall; Bright sunlight from a window (or a glass prism if you have one)
steps: Place the tray of water where sunlight from a window reaches it.
Slide the mirror into the water, leaning it against one side at an angle.
Adjust the mirror so sunlight strikes the underwater part and reflects up onto the white paper or wall.
The wedge of water in front of the mirror acts as a prism. Look for a band of colours on the paper.
Record the colours you see and their order.

activities.title: Why Objects Have Colour
activities.materials: A torch; Coloured see-through sweet wrappers or thin coloured plastic (red, blue, green); Small squares of coloured cloth or coloured paper (red, blue, green, white, black); A dark room
steps: Cover the torch with a red wrapper to make a red beam.
In a dark room, shine the red light on each coloured cloth in turn and record its apparent colour.
Repeat with a blue wrapper, then a green wrapper.
Note especially what happens to a cloth whose colour is NOT in the light you are shining.

activities.title: Observe: Dispersion: The Hidden Colours of White Light
activities.materials: Three pieces of card or stiff paper (a cereal box works well); A torch or a phone torch; A pencil, a ruler, and some sticky tack or small lumps of dough to stand the cards up
steps: Look for an example of dispersion: the hidden colours of white light around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Luminous and Non-luminous.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Always Measure From the Normal
rules.text: Always measure angles from the NORMAL, not from the mirror surface. A very common mistake is to read the angle off the mirror. If a question gives you the angle to the surface, subtract it from 90 to get the angle of incidence.

rules.title: Protect Your Eyes From the Sun
rules.text: Never look directly at the sun, and never let anyone reflect sunlight into your eyes with a mirror. The strong equatorial sun can permanently damage the retina in seconds, and you feel no pain to warn you. Wear a hat or sunglasses in strong sun. Protecting the eyes you were given is a duty of care.

realProblems.prompt: Amina sees a shimmering 'pool of water' on the hot road to Garissa that disappears as she nears it. Explain what she is really seeing and why.
realProblems.answer: She is seeing a mirage. Hot, thin air just above the tarmac bends (refracts) light from the sky upward into her eyes, so an image of the bright sky appears on the road and looks like water. There is no real water.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Luminous, Non-luminous, Ray — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: She is seeing a mirage. Hot, thin air just above the tarmac bends (refracts) light from the sky upward into her eyes, so an image of the bright sky appears on the road and looks like water. There is no real water.

realProblems.prompt: A fisherman near Kismaayo aims his spear below where a fish appears to be. Explain why this helps him.
realProblems.answer: Refraction bends the light from the fish as it leaves the water, so the fish appears higher and in a slightly different place than it truly is. Aiming below the apparent position corrects for the bend.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Luminous, Non-luminous, Ray — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Refraction bends the light from the fish as it leaves the water, so the fish appears higher and in a slightly different place than it truly is. Aiming below the apparent position corrects for the bend.

realProblems.prompt: Halima buys a cloth that looks a rich blue by the red glow of a market lamp but looks almost black in the shop's dim red light. Explain what is happening.
realProblems.answer: An object can only reflect colours present in the light. The lamp gives mostly red light, so a blue cloth has almost no blue to reflect and looks nearly black. In true daylight, which contains blue, it would look blue again.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Luminous, Non-luminous, Ray — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: An object can only reflect colours present in the light. The lamp gives mostly red light, so a blue cloth has almost no blue to reflect and looks nearly black. In true daylight, which contains blue, it would look blue again.

realProblems.prompt: Explain why wearing a white robe keeps you cooler in the strong equatorial sun than wearing a black one.
realProblems.answer: White reflects all colours and absorbs little, so it stays cool; black absorbs almost all light and turns it to heat, so a black robe gets hot.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Luminous, Non-luminous, Ray — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: White reflects all colours and absorbs little, so it stays cool; black absorbs almost all light and turns it to heat, so a black robe gets hot.

realProblems.prompt: After the Gu rains the sun breaks through and a rainbow arches over the savanna. Explain, step by step, how the rainbow forms in the raindrops.
realProblems.answer: Sunlight enters each raindrop and refracts, splits into colours by dispersion, reflects off the back of the drop, and refracts again on the way out. Millions of drops each send a colour to your eyes, forming the arch. You see it with the sun behind you and rain in front.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Luminous, Non-luminous, Ray — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Sunlight enters each raindrop and refracts, splits into colours by dispersion, reflects off the back of the drop, and refracts again on the way out. Millions of drops each send a colour to your eyes, forming the arch. You see it with the sun behind you and rain in front.

realProblems.prompt: A ray of light strikes a flat mirror making an angle of 65 degrees with the mirror surface. Find the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection, showing your working.
realProblems.answer: The angle is given from the surface, so the angle of incidence = 90 — 65 = 25 degrees. By the law of reflection the angle of reflection = 25 degrees (both from the normal).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a luminous and a non-luminous object? Give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A luminous object makes its own light (e.g. the sun, a fire); a non-luminous object does not and is seen by reflected light (e.g. the moon, a goat).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: State the law of reflection in one sentence.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must angles in reflection be measured from the normal and not from the mirror?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because the normal gives a fixed 90-degree reference. Measuring from the tilted mirror surface would give inconsistent, confusing angles.
Refraction is the bending of light as it changes speed when passing from one transparent material into another.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A straw in a glass of water looks bent. Explain why using the idea of refraction.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Light from the underwater part of the straw refracts (bends) as it leaves the water into the air, so the straw's lower part appears shifted, making it look bent or broken at the surface.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the two types of lens and say whether each brings light together or spreads it out.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A convex (converging) lens brings light together; a concave (diverging) lens spreads light out.

rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Dispersion splits white light into its spectrum of colours.

rounds.prompt: A blue cloth under pure red light looks:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: black. There is no blue light in a red beam for the blue cloth to reflect, so it looks black.

rounds.prompt: The imaginary line at 90 degrees to a mirror is called the:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: normal. The normal is drawn at 90 degrees to the surface and is the reference for all angles.

rounds.prompt: The bending of light as it passes from air into water is called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed between materials.

games.title: Spot the Error: Concave lens
games.description: Practise concave lens through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: The three primary colours of LIGHT are:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: red, green, blue. These are the primary colours of light; they add to make white.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a luminous object?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the sun. A luminous object makes its own light; the moon, a mirror and a mango only reflect light.

rounds.prompt: The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: reflection. The law states angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

rounds.prompt: A convex lens is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: thicker in the middle. A convex (converging) lens is thicker at its centre.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Dispersion
games.description: Practise dispersion through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A red cloth looks red because it:
choices: absorbs red and reflects the rest
reflects red and absorbs the rest
rounds.answer: reflects red and absorbs the rest
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: reflects red and absorbs the rest. The cloth reflects only red light to your eyes.

rounds.prompt: Light travels in:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: straight lines. This is shown by sharp shadows and narrow beams.

rounds.prompt: A ray hits a mirror at 30 degrees to the normal. The angle of reflection is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: 30 degrees. By the law of reflection the reflected angle equals the incident angle.

rounds.prompt: The part of the eye where the image forms is the:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: retina. The image forms on the light-sensitive retina at the back of the eye.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit you will be able to:
I can explain that light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines and describe evidence for this, such as shadows and beams.
I can describe the difference between luminous and non-luminous objects and explain how we see non-luminous objects by reflected light.
I can state and use the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
I can measure angles of incidence and reflection from the normal and solve simple numerical problems.
I can explain refraction as the bending of light when it changes speed passing from one material into another.
I can describe how convex and concave lenses bend light, and explain how a converging lens forms an image.
I can label the main parts of the human eye and explain how the eye focuses light onto the retina.
